entries.name: Equalized odds
entries.definition: A fairness criterion requiring a predictor's output to be conditionally independent of a specified protected attribute given the target outcome; for binary predictions and outcomes, it requires equal true-positive and false-positive rates across the compared groups.
entries.identity_notes: This is the distributional criterion in Hardt, Price and Srebro's Definition 2.1, not their postprocessing algorithm, a bias type, demographic parity or a claim of overall social fairness. Equal opportunity is a weaker positive-outcome-only constraint. All 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 94 preceding native identities were compared, with ignored-inclusive text searches in both checkouts.
entries.mechanism: Assess whether the conditional distribution of the prediction given the outcome is the same across protected groups. In the binary case, test both P(prediction=1 | A=a,Y=1) and P(prediction=1 | A=a,Y=0) across a. The general independence definition also applies to scores and nonbinary variables; thresholding an equalized-odds score by a common rule preserves the property.
entries.locator: Section 2, Definition 2.1, PDF p. 3; Sections 2.2–2.3, PDF p. 4; Section 6, PDF pp. 12–14; discussion of reliable targets and nonconclusive fairness tests, PDF pp. 20–21
entries.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
entries.mapping_rationale: The criterion constrains classifier predictions and error rates in its central binary setting. Classification denotes the prediction task; equalized odds denotes a condition used to assess its outputs, so this is a direct task/criterion relationship rather than equivalence or subclassing.
limitations: The conditioning outcome and protected groups must be specified, with estimable nonzero-probability conditioning strata for rate comparisons. Biased or unreliable outcome labels can undermine interpretation.

Equal true-positive and false-positive rates do not require identical overall accuracy when group outcome prevalences differ. The record uses the formal conditional-independence definition, not the source's informal equal-accuracy wording.

This is an oblivious distributional test: identical prediction/outcome/group statistics can arise from different underlying dependency structures. Satisfaction or violation alone is not conclusive evidence of overall fairness or unfairness.
Finite-sample uncertainty, a tolerance and domain-specific interpretation are needed in an application; no empirical result, universal fairness guarantee or legal-compliance claim is asserted.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes observable distributional criteria and a separate postprocessing construction, with explicit limits on what the criteria establish. Records represent conditions, not the algorithm or a universal judgment of fairness.

entries.name: Equal opportunity in binary classification
entries.definition: A binary-classification fairness criterion requiring equal probabilities of a positive prediction across specified protected groups among individuals whose target outcome is the designated positive outcome.
entries.identity_notes: The identity is Hardt, Price and Srebro's Definition 2.2, with the positive target designated as the advantaged outcome. It is not the wider philosophical meaning of equal opportunity, the full equalized-odds condition, or a threshold-adjustment algorithm. Identity searches covered all 442 AIO labels and scoped synonyms, 94 preceding native records and ignored/hidden-inclusive text in both checkouts.
entries.mechanism: For each compared protected group a, evaluate P(prediction=1 | A=a,Y=1) and require equality across groups. This constrains true-positive rates and imposes no corresponding equality requirement at Y=0. It relaxes the binary equalized-odds criterion by retaining only the designated positive-outcome condition.
entries.locator: Section 2.1, Definition 2.2, PDF p. 4; Section 2, Definition 2.1, PDF p. 3; Section 6, PDF pp. 12–14; reliable-target and interpretation discussion, PDF pp. 20–21
entries.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
entries.mapping_rationale: The criterion directly constrains true-positive rates of binary classifiers. BinaryClassification is the task on which the condition is evaluated; it is not a broader class of fairness criteria or an equivalent identity.
limitations: The definition depends on which target outcome is designated positive/advantaged; changing that designation changes the constrained population.
Equal opportunity alone does not equalize false-positive rates, selection rates, predictive values or individual treatment.
The criterion requires meaningful target labels and sufficiently supported group/positive-outcome strata. Finite-sample uncertainty is not eliminated by writing an equality.
Like other oblivious criteria, this condition does not determine the causal process or establish overall social fairness, empirical utility or legal compliance.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes observable distributional criteria and a separate postprocessing construction, with explicit limits on what the criteria establish. Records represent conditions, not the algorithm or a universal judgment of fairness.

entries.name: Demographic parity
entries.definition: A group-level prediction criterion requiring the distribution of a decision or prediction to be independent of a specified protected attribute; for a binary decision, the positive-decision rate is equal across the compared groups.
entries.identity_notes: The record denotes exact distributional parity, also called statistical parity in the inspected fairness literature. It is not equalized odds, equality of true-positive rates, an approximate disparity tolerance, or a complete fairness judgment. All 442 AIO identities/scoped synonyms, 94 native identities and ignored-inclusive text in both checkouts were searched. Conditional parity and parity for selected subgroups require separately stated conditioning and scope.
entries.mechanism: Compare the prediction distributions conditional on each protected group without conditioning on the target outcome. In binary classification the condition reduces to equality of P(prediction=1 | A=a) across groups. For the statistical-parity formulation of Dwork and colleagues, exact parity is the zero-tolerance case in which the total-variation distance between group output distributions vanishes.
entries.locator: Section 1, demographic-parity definition and limitations, PDF pp. 1–2
entries.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
entries.mapping_rationale: Demographic parity directly constrains the distribution of classifier decisions across groups. Classification is a task to which this output criterion applies, not an equivalent criterion or a bias type; the mapping does not limit the mathematical independence condition to binary outputs.
limitations: Matching group output rates does not ensure similar individuals receive similar treatment or that parity holds within every subgroup.

If target outcomes have different prevalences by group, a perfectly accurate predictor can violate demographic parity. This statistical observation does not by itself choose which fairness criterion a domain should use.
Exact independence is distinct from approximate parity within a specified tolerance; an empirical estimate needs uncertainty and population context.

Connections to counterfactual fairness depend on causal-model assumptions and how the predictor/model is constructed. Shared population statistics do not make the two definitions interchangeable for a fixed causal model.

entries.name: Lipschitz individual fairness
entries.definition: An individual-fairness criterion requiring the distance between the output distributions assigned by a randomized classifier to any two individuals to be no greater than their task-specific similarity distance.
entries.identity_notes: The record is the explicit (D,d)-Lipschitz condition in Dwork and colleagues' framework. It is narrower than every possible notion of individual fairness and separate from their loss-minimizing linear-program construction, metric-learning algorithms, differential privacy and group parity. Identity assessment covered 442 AIO labels/scoped synonyms, 94 preceding native identities and ignored-inclusive searches of both checkouts.
entries.mechanism: Given a mapping M from individuals to distributions over outcomes, an externally specified task distance d and an output-distribution distance D, require D(M(x),M(y)) <= d(x,y) for every compared pair. The criterion constrains permissible mappings; choosing among them requires a separate utility objective. The paper studies total-variation and relative-l-infinity output distances as particular choices.
entries.locator: Sections 1.1–1.2, printed pp. 1–3 / PDF pp. 2–4; Section 2, Definition 2.1 and equation (1), printed p. 4 / PDF p. 5; Section 2.1 probability metrics and Remark 2.1, printed p. 5 / PDF p. 6
entries.title: Fairness Through Awareness
entries.version: arXiv:1104.3913v2, revised 2011-11-29; downloaded PDF title-page date 2024-11-26
entries.mapping_rationale: The condition directly constrains randomized classifiers' outcome distributions. Classification denotes the task while this local concept denotes a constraint on its mapping, so related_match preserves the abstraction difference. MetricLearning is not a substitute: the defining criterion assumes a task metric rather than specifying a neural procedure that learns one.
limitations: The task-specific distance and output-distance choice determine the constraint. The framework does not certify that a chosen similarity metric represents an appropriate social or domain judgment.
A constant output distribution satisfies the condition; useful predictions require a separate utility objective. Criterion satisfaction alone does not guarantee predictive quality.

The formulation over an inspected finite population does not itself guarantee generalization to unobserved individuals. Group-parity implications require additional conditions on the metric and group distributions.
This record does not equate the criterion with all individual-fairness notions, certify the paper's full optimization/theorem results, or assert legal compliance.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes task-specific similarity constraints on randomized classification and utility optimization subject to them. The criterion assumes a domain distance rather than certifying its normative appropriateness.

entries.name: Counterfactual fairness
entries.definition: A fairness criterion in a specified causal model requiring a predictor's conditional output distribution, given an individual's observed attributes and protected-attribute value, to remain unchanged under counterfactual interventions that assign other attainable protected-attribute values.
entries.identity_notes: This is Kusner and colleagues' Definition 5, an equality of conditional counterfactual distributions. It is not merely changing an input feature while freezing its causal descendants, a group-level observational equality, the FAIRLEARNING algorithm, or a generic guarantee of social fairness. All 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms, 94 preceding native identities and ignored-inclusive text in both checkouts were searched. Later parity connections do not establish identity under an arbitrary fixed causal model.
entries.mechanism: Condition on the factual context X=x,A=a to infer background-variable uncertainty; replace the protected-attribute structural assignment by a counterfactual value and propagate that intervention through the causal model. Compare the resulting prediction distributions for all attainable protected values while retaining the same factual conditioning context. The criterion is distributional, and the paper gives using non-descendants of the protected attributes as a sufficient construction, not a necessary restriction on all possible predictors.
entries.locator: Section 2.2 and Section 3, Definition 5/equation (1), PDF p. 3; Section 3.2, Lemma 1 and its qualification, PDF p. 5; Sections 4.2–4.3, causal assumptions and interpretive limits, PDF p. 7
entries.title: Counterfactual Fairness
entries.mapping_rationale: The criterion is defined and assessed using a structural causal model that encodes the data-generating assumptions. AIO CausalGraphicalModel describes that supporting model type; the criterion itself is neither a graphical model nor an equivalent causal graph.
limitations: The comparison depends on causal and counterfactual assumptions that observational data alone generally cannot establish. Specifying protected attributes and meaningful interventions requires domain interpretation.

Ignoring protected attributes as explicit inputs is insufficient when other inputs carry their causal effects. Conversely, using a descendant is not categorically excluded if the relevant total dependence cancels, as the source qualifies its sufficient construction.

A predictor satisfying the condition in an assumed model need not satisfy it under a model with omitted confounding; the inspected sensitivity paper studies this vulnerability in additive-noise models.

The criterion constrains conditional output distributions, not necessarily pointwise equality for every unobserved state or usefulness of a predictor. Connections to demographic parity retain their model/independence assumptions.

source_caveats.source: Hardt et al. Definition 2.1 and following informal text, PDF p. 3
source_caveats.observation: Formal equalized odds constrains conditional error rates. The adjacent informal claim of equal accuracy across demographics is not adopted: with TPR=.9 and FPR=.2, outcome prevalences .2 and .8 yield accuracies .82 and .88 respectively. This is a curator mathematical counterexample, not a benchmark result.
Criteria 3 independence and the constructed-model direction are explicit. The paper itself distinguishes a fixed causal model. Its title is not used to merge criterion identities.

Hardt arXiv v1 is dated 2016-10-07 in the repository while its downloaded title page says 2016-10-11. Dwork arXiv v2 is dated 2011-11-29 while its title page says 2024-11-26. Exact versions, observed title dates and downloaded hashes are retained without asserting a new publication date.

The AAAI DOI open returned an internal error and direct PDF download closed the connection. The publisher landing page and exact arXiv v4 were subsequently accessed; no paywall or access control was bypassed.
Definitions and inspected limitations are curated. Complete proof correctness, normative suitability, legal compliance and empirical model fairness are not certified.
